title: Aad sach: the sound
hookLine: aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhi sach, Nanak hosi bhi sach

cards: Four little claims, and the same word landing at the end of each one, like a drum hitting the same beat four times. That's the shape of the short verse right after the title, jap: a salok, just two lines long.

It's sung as well as recited. You'll hear it at the start of Japji every morning, and at gatherings as kirtan, sung round and round until the whole room is singing. You can feel its shape before you know a single word.

teach.b: Here it is, slowly. Aad sach. Jugaad sach.
Hai bhee sach. Naanak hosee bhee sach. Listen for the word that keeps coming back: sach.
It sounds a little like such, said softly. That's the drumbeat. Now the pieces.
Aad: a long a, as in father. Jugaad: ju-GAAD, and inside it is jug, an age, a great stretch of time. Hai bhee: hai, like high, and bhee, like bee with a breath on the b.
Naanak: the Guru's own name, NAA-nak.
Hosee bhee: HO-see bhee. Now the shape. The first line is two short pairs: aad sach, jugaad sach.
The second stretches out, three beats, then four, as if the verse leans forward. And hear what the pieces sound like before you know them: aad, a beginning; jug, the ages; hai, is; hosee, will be.
It moves from before, through the long ages, to right now, and on into what's coming.
In every line, the same word holds still while the time around it moves.

The sound is teaching before the meaning arrives; what sach means, and what the four lines claim, comes tomorrow. In Gurmukhi, sach carries the same small silent mark under its last letter that you saw on jap.
Sangats often sing this salok as simple kirtan, and with one word coming back four times, it's easy to join.

how: The salok 'aad sach, jugaad sach' follows the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji; sangats also sing it as simple kirtan, repeating it many times.

games.q: match the sound to its piece.
p: an age, a stretch of time

s: the salok after the Mool Mantar is two lines long
aad sach, jugaad sach; hai bhee sach, Naanak hosee bhee sach.
the word sach appears only once
it lands four times, like a drumbeat.
this salok is only recited, never sung
sangats often sing it as simple kirtan, round and round.

games.q: you're hearing the salok for the first time. which word keeps coming back?
games.why: sach, four times, holding still while the time around it moves.

practice: Say it four times, out loud if you can: aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhee sach, Naanak hosee bhee sach. Each round a little slower and softer, letting sach land, until the last is almost a whisper.
Then sit, let the last sach fade, and notice your breath went on the whole time underneath the words; if you pray, you can stay with Waheguru in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Aad sach. The opening words of the salok after the Mool Mantar. One word, sach, holds the whole verse up.

carryVoice: Your line: let the last sach fade. The week behind you: a shield for others, your rhythm, the Guru's alphabet, Japji Sahib, the Mool Mantar and jap. Day one hundred sixty-one, done.
